title: Read and write paths
summary: Draw one successful read and one successful write end to end.

parts.rule: For the core use case, narrate one successful write and one successful read from the client to durable storage and back. Name every hop: load balancer, application, cache, primary, replica. Say which row or object key is touched. Keep the first diagram limited to these two paths before adding fanout workers or analytics side cars.
parts.why: Boxes without a walked path are decoration. Path narration exposes missing ownership, synchronous choke points, and where latency hides. Interviewers often ask you to follow a single request; being ready is the difference between a calm answer and a scramble.
parts.example: Shortener write path: client sends POST /links with a long URL; API validates; app generates code a1b2c3d; primary database inserts the links row; response returns the code. Shortener read path: client sends GET /a1b2c3d; API checks cache; on miss, primary or read replica selects by code; cache is filled; HTTP 302 returns the long URL. Feed read path: GET /feed loads precomputed timeline rows for that user_id. The asynchronous hop is visible on the write story instead of hiding inside a vague feed-service box with no arrows. body:
Rule. For the core use case, narrate one successful write and one successful read from the client to durable storage and back. Name every hop: load balancer, application, cache, primary, replica. Say which row or object key is touched. Keep the first diagram limited to these two paths before adding fanout workers or analytics side cars.

Why it matters. Boxes without a walked path are decoration. Path narration exposes missing ownership, synchronous choke points, and where latency hides. Interviewers often ask you to follow a single request; being ready is the difference between a calm answer and a scramble.

Worked example. Shortener write path: client sends POST /links with a long URL; API validates; app generates code a1b2c3d; primary database inserts the links row; response returns the code. Shortener read path: client sends GET /a1b2c3d; API checks cache; on miss, primary or read replica selects by code; cache is filled; HTTP 302 returns the long URL. Feed write path: client posts; API inserts the post row; a fanout job is enqueued; HTTP 201 returns before follower timelines update. Feed read path: GET /feed loads precomputed timeline rows for that user_id. The asynchronous hop is visible on the write story instead of hiding inside a vague feed-service box with no arrows. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool.

When to use. Draw both paths right after the data model. Use them to place caches and queues deliberately rather than by habit. Re-walk the path whenever someone adds a dependency mid-interview.

When to refuse. Refuse a diagram with ten services and zero request walks. Refuse adding a cache before the uncached path is clear. Refuse merging read and write into one vague bidirectional arrow. Refuse omitting the row key the path actually uses.
